summary: In an ordinary agno agent, the AI model decides at every turn whether to call tools or answer, and plain code runs every tool call it asks for without asking a person unless the developer marked that tool. The run ends when the model replies without asking for a tool, and by default nothing checks that answer, so even a reply cut off by the token limit is reported as completed.

judgments.question: When an agent is built without a model, which model answers its requests?
judgments.answer: OpenAI's gpt-5.4 through the Responses API; any model the developer passes wins.

judgments.question: May a tool call the model issued run, without a person being asked?
judgments.answer: Yes. Code runs every tool call the model makes; it pauses for a person only on tools the developer marked for confirmation, user input or external execution, or on the ask-the-person tools when those are added.

judgments.question: Approve or reject this paused tool call?
judgments.answer: Only for a tool marked for confirmation: the run pauses and returns, the developer's code collects the person's yes or no and continues the run, and a missing answer counts as a no.

judgments.question: Should the agent stop and ask the person?
judgments.answer: Only when the developer adds agno's ask-the-person toolkits; then the model decides when to stop and ask, and the run pauses for the person.

judgments.question: After this turn, is the run over, or does the agent take another turn?
judgments.answer: The model decides: agno keeps calling it while it asks for tools and stops when a reply has none, with no turn limit by default.

judgments.question: Before an agent's answer is returned, does anything check that it is right or complete?
judgments.answer: Nothing, by default. The reply that ends the run is returned as completed; a check runs only if the developer adds post-hooks such as guardrails or evals.

judgments.question: Is the model's reply complete, or was it cut off or refused?
judgments.answer: The shared run loop does not turn a reply cut off by the token limit, or refused, into anything but a completed run: whatever text came back is the answer. Some provider adapters log a warning.

judgments.question: When an agent keeps asking for tools, when are further tool calls refused?
judgments.answer: No limit by default. With a tool-call limit set, calls past it are not run and the model is told so; the run goes on.

judgments.question: Which earlier messages of this conversation are replayed to the model?
judgments.answer: None by default; with history switched on and a database, the last 3 runs of the session, or the count the developer sets.

judgments.question: Has the history grown enough that older turns should be folded into a summary?
judgments.answer: Off by default. A Compaction object folds once replayed history reaches 150,000 tokens; compaction=True folds only after the provider rejects a request as too long.

judgments.question: When a tool fails, what does the model see, and does the run go on?
judgments.answer: The error text goes back to the model as the tool's result and the model decides what next; the run does not fail.

judgments.question: In a team, which member should take this piece of the work?
judgments.answer: In the default coordinate mode the team leader's model picks the member for each sub-task from the members' roles and descriptions.

problems.title: A reply cut off by the token limit is reported as completed
problems.plain: The run ends as soon as the model replies without asking for a tool, and the shared run loop does not look at why the model stopped (some provider adapters only log a warning). So an answer cut short by the output-token limit, or refused, comes back as the answer with the run marked completed, and the caller cannot tell it from a finished one. An open pull request proposes reporting the provider's stop reason.

problems.title: A structured answer that does not parse still counts as success
problems.plain: When the developer asks for a structured answer and the model's text cannot be turned into it, agno keeps the raw text, logs a warning, and still marks the run completed. Code that expects the structured object gets plain text instead unless it checks the type itself. An open pull request proposes an opt-in way to report the failure.

problems.title: Later workflow steps can lose the user's original request
problems.plain: From the second step of a workflow on, an agent or team step receives only the previous step's output, not what the user first asked; the original request reaches it only when the previous step produced nothing. The function's own description says it combines the two, so a step can end up working without the user's question in front of it.
